results.summary: It sequentially enables and disables eight output channels with a configurable delay set by five delay input bits. Counters and registers track the activation state and threshold for each channel. After reset, raising enable starts channel 0 and proceeds upward, while lowering enable turns channels off starting from channel 7 downward. No external hardware is required, though the design could be used for GaAs amplifiers or other circuits that need sequenced power supplies.

It is a simple UART transmitter that sends 8-bit parallel data at 115200 baud. The user presents data on ui[7:0] and asserts tx_send, after which the module transmits on TX and indicates busy. It requires only a clock and an external UART receiver or serial interface to observe the output. The documentation is minimal and does not describe parity, stop bits, or flow control beyond the basic transmit behavior.

It implements a PWM modulator in Verilog with an 8-bit duty-cycle input and a single PWM output. The documentation is largely a restatement of the one-line description and does not provide detailed timing, resolution, or test results. It is intended to regulate energy delivered to a device and is tested using a Xilinx Basys 3 FPGA. No external hardware or silicon test report is described.

It generates a PWM waveform whose duty cycle is set by a 7-bit input on ui_in[6:0]. An internal counter increments each clock and is compared with the duty value to keep the output high while the counter is below it. The design provides two identical PWM outputs and is tested by observing the waveform on an oscilloscope or logic analyzer. It requires only a clock and external measurement equipment, and no silicon test results are provided.

It plays the Super Mario tune through a piezo speaker using differential PWM outputs. The design was generated by converting an RTTL ringtone into Verilog with Python and runs from a 100 kHz clock. After a brief reset pulse, it drives uo[0] and uo[1] as a differential sound wave. It requires an external piezo speaker connected across those two outputs and has no reported silicon test results.

It is a Verilog replica of the General Instrument AY-3-8913 three-voice programmable sound generator. It implements square-wave tone generators, a white-noise LFSR, an envelope generator, 16 volume levels, and a register interface over a multiplexed data/address bus. It outputs either 8-bit digital audio for an external DAC or PWM audio for an RC filter or op-amp, and it can be driven by a microcontroller. Silicon test reports indicate it works, including use with an audio Pmod and chiptune playback from YM register files.

It is a digital PWM generator with selectable 5- to 9-bit resolution, dyadic modulation, and three dithering modes. A 12-bit control word sets duty cycle, and the design produces complementary high-side and low-side outputs with dead-time plus a sync clock. Configuration is written through pins into a small register file, and the default after reset is 8-bit normal PWM. It is intended for power-electronics use such as a half-bridge gate driver, and a cocotb testbench exercises its modes.

It implements a spiking neural network with STDP and reward-based learning in Verilog. The design is described as eight layers built from two-neuron loops, with 4-bit weights loaded from memory. Testing involves loading 32 weights with layer and node addresses, then applying two input values to execute. The documentation is very thin and does not explain the learning rule, interfaces, or expected outputs in detail.

It is described as an AXI-Stream matrix-vector multiplier with a UART interface. The only pins are UART RX and TX, and the provided documentation refers to an external GitHub repository rather than describing the design. It requires an external USB-FTDI interface for UART communication. Because the local documentation is essentially absent, its internal architecture, matrix dimensions, and test results cannot be assessed.

Basic8 is a minimal 8-bit CPU with eight general-purpose registers, an ALU, branches, and JAL. Instructions are 16 bits and are loaded in two cycles through ui_in, with uio_in[0] latching the high byte and uio_in[1] executing the combined instruction. The program counter is output on uo_out so an external ROM can supply instructions based on the current PC. It requires no external hardware beyond the driving controller, and a cocotb testbench covers the instruction set.
